newsitem.title: ZAIRE: FEATURE-War strangles Upper Zaire's jungle economy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-War strangles Upper Zaire's jungle economy.

text.p: War in eastern Zaire is destroying what is left of Upper Zaire's jungle economy, forcing prices beyond the reach of its impoverished inhabitants and threatening to halt the region's trade in gems and gold.

At the head of the navigable part of the vast Zaire River, Kisangani was once considered Zaire's second port, and the heart of the region's trade in agricultural, timber and textile products as well as gold and minerals.

But with the eastern Kivu provinces blocked off by rebel occupation since November, and river traders afraid to travel up the 1,500 kilometres from the capital to a war zone, the region is increasingly asphyxiated on all fronts.

"There is almost nothing left standing. It is more than a war situation here. The war has simply come to finish off what years of decline have already started. We have literally to reconstruct the country from zero," one of Kisangani's leading businessmen, told Reuters.
Given a lack of passable roads through Zaire's vast tracts of jungle and bush, the Zaire River and its many tributaries remain the principle arteries for the country's internal and external trade.
At Kisangani's rusting port, officials estimate that traffic which should be peaking now with waters at a seasonal high, has declined by two thirds since fighting in the east broke out last October.
SHIPPERS AFRAID OF INSECURITY

"Most of the shipping companies are afraid to bring their boats here. They are afraid they will lose their cargo," says Jean-Jacques Kime, deputy director of the local branch of the ONATRA state transport company.
Sporadic bouts of army-led looting since the beginning of Zaire's transition to democracy in 1990 have sent most of the region's expatriate businesses elsewhere.

Most recently, demoralised and hungry soldiers fleeing the rebel invasion in the Kivu provinces tore through the region looting and destroying the few remaining trading posts and stock depots in their path, and stealing hundreds of heavy trucks.

"In almost every town with a sizeable population everything in sight was looted and demolished. It is a catastrophic situation as far as commerce is concerned. And even schools and hospitals don't exist anymore," said Father Jerry Selenke, a Kansas-born American missionary who has lived in Kisangani for 13 years.
Kisangani is known as Zaire's third city, with a population the governor, Lombeya Bosongo, estimates at close to half a million.
But apart from a few crumbling buildings at the town centre it now resembles less a city than a series of forest villages.
LOCALS OPT FOR SELF-SUFFICIENCY

Abandoned by the central state during years of nationwide economic decline, inhabitants, amongst them university graduates and professors, have increasingly turned to planting vegetables around their mud houses to survive.

Even the trade in gold and diamonds, which aside from the city's thousands of bicycle taxis is one of the few remaining options the young and unemployed have for an independent living, have been hit hard by the latest crisis.
In the city centre, Lebanese-run diamond counters, painted with bright hoardings to draw in rugged artesanal miners from the bush, have been barred shut.

"The diamonds come from the bush, but the guys who go to dig for them are now afraid because of the insecurity, and soldiers who steal their diamonds and money," James Mbuyamba, one of a handful of Zairean dealers left in town, told Reuters.

"What we made before in the wink of an eye, we now make in week. And for those who dig the diamonds, their capital is in their muscle. Since they are not labouring they too are earning nothing," he added.
As supplies of food dwindle, prices rise. Market traders who once bicycled miles into the surrounding bush and jungle to fetch produce now only dare to pedal within Kisangani's perimeters.
NEW ARRIVALS AN ADDED PROBLEM
Tens of thousands of displaced Zaireans have swollen the local population after fleeing fighting further east, and have added pressure to the dwindling supplies.

If inhabitants of the region are not yet starving, said one leading businessman, it is because Zaire is a scandal of riches, where chickens let loose in the yard multiply, and where fish and fruit are free of charge for those desperate enough to revert to hunting and gathering.
